docs.title: Hospital Identity & Access Integration Project
docs.text:
Build it. Break it. Troubleshoot it. Understand it.

Welcome to a beginner-friendly, hands-on project where you will build a small simulated hospital IT environment and gradually integrate a new software application into it.

Safe learning environment

This project uses fictional users and simulated infrastructure. No real hospital systems, patient data, or production credentials are used.

docs.title: Your Mission
docs.text:
Imagine you have joined the technical implementation team of a hospital.

The hospital needs an IT environment that can:

  • manage doctors, nurses, pharmacy staff, and IT users
  • authenticate employees
  • control access to resources
  • support new software applications
  • integrate applications with existing identity systems
  • be investigated when something goes wrong

You will build that environment step by step.

docs.title: What You Will Build
docs.text:
Host Computer
(Windows, macOS, or Linux)
        │
        └── Virtualization Platform
                │
                ├── Windows Server 2022 VM
                │      │
                │      ├── Active Directory
                │      ├── DNS
                │      ├── Users & OUs
                │      ├── Security Groups
                │      └── SMB Access Control
                │
                └── Ubuntu Integration VM
                       │
                       ├── Network Testing
                       ├── DNS Queries
                       ├── LDAP
                       └── Software Integration

The exact virtualization software you use may depend on your host operating system.

For example, you might use VMware Fusion on macOS, VMware Workstation on Windows or Linux, or another virtualization platform capable of running the required virtual machines.

The important part of this project is the architecture and concepts, not the brand of hypervisor.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
By working through the project, you will gain hands-on experience with:

  • virtualization and virtual machines
  • Windows Server 2022
  • Active Directory Domain Services
  • DNS and IP networking
  • Identity and Access Management
  • authentication and authorization
  • Organizational Units and Security Groups
  • SMB and NTFS permissions
  • Ubuntu Linux
  • LDAP
  • service accounts
  • PowerShell
  • troubleshooting
  • enterprise software integration

docs.title: Part 1 — Build the Environment
docs.text:
01. Virtualization Setup Create the virtual machines that will form the hospital environment.

02. Windows Server Prepare the Windows Server that will become the Domain Controller.

03. Networking Configure IP addressing, DNS, connectivity, and time synchronization.

docs.title: Part 2 — Identity & Access
docs.text:
04. Active Directory Build the hospital.local domain and create the hospital identity structure.

05. Access Management Create users, Security Groups, and test authorization.

06. SMB & Permissions Protect hospital resources using group-based access control.

docs.title: Part 3 — Integration
docs.text:
07. Ubuntu Integration Machine Introduce a Linux system that will act as an external integration machine.

08. LDAP Integration Allow an external system to query identities from Active Directory.

docs.title: Coming Next
docs.text:
The project will later expand into:

  • application-level integration
  • SQL and database integration
  • PowerShell automation
  • provisioning and deprovisioning
  • LDAPS / TLS
  • client workstations
  • troubleshooting challenges

docs.title: How This Project Teaches
docs.text:
This is not a "copy commands and hope they work" tutorial.

For each stage, we will ask:

  1. What are we building?
  2. Why is it needed?
  3. How do we configure it?
  4. How do we verify it?
  5. What could go wrong?
  6. What did we learn?

Real problems encountered while building the environment are preserved as troubleshooting exercises.

Authentication vs Authorization

We configured an SMB clinical folder for nurses.

Emma was a member of GG-Nurses and could access the resource.

Marie had a valid Active Directory account but was not a member of the required group, so access was denied.

Both users could have valid identities, but only one was authorized to access the resource.

docs.title: Ready?
docs.text:
Start with Virtualization Setup →

Project status: Work in progress

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
In this lesson, you will create the virtual environment that will host our simulated hospital infrastructure.

By the end, you will have two virtual machines:

  • a Windows Server 2022 VM
  • an Ubuntu integration VM

These machines will later communicate with each other as if they were separate computers inside a hospital network.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
You need a computer capable of running virtual machines.

The host computer can run:

  • Windows
  • macOS
  • Linux

You will also need a virtualisation platform.

Examples include:

  • VMware Fusion
  • VMware Workstation
  • VirtualBox
  • Hyper-V
  • another hypervisor capable of running the required guest operating systems

Note

This project was originally built using VMware Fusion, but VMware Fusion is not required.

The screenshots and menus you see may differ depending on your virtualisation software.

What matters is that you understand the architecture and can create virtual machines that communicate with each other.

docs.title: What Is Virtualisation?
docs.text:
Normally, one physical computer runs one operating system.

Virtualisation allows one physical computer to run several independent computers at the same time.

Your physical computer is called the host.

The software that creates and manages virtual machines is called a hypervisor.

The operating systems running inside the virtual machines are called guest operating systems.

Our environment will look like this:

Physical Computer
        │
        └── Hypervisor
                │
                ├── Windows Server 2022 VM
                │
                └── Ubuntu VM

Each virtual machine gets its own:

  • virtual CPU
  • memory
  • disk
  • network adapter
  • operating system

To the operating system inside the VM, these virtual resources behave much like physical hardware.

docs.title: Host
docs.text: The physical computer running the virtualisation software.

docs.title: Hypervisor
docs.text:
Software that creates and manages virtual machines.

Examples include VMware, VirtualBox, and Hyper-V.

docs.title: Virtual Machine
docs.text: A software-defined computer running inside the host computer.

docs.title: Guest Operating System
docs.text:
The operating system installed inside a virtual machine.

In this project our guest operating systems include Windows Server and Ubuntu.

docs.title: ISO Image
docs.text:
An ISO is a file containing installation media for an operating system.

It acts like a virtual installation DVD.

docs.title: Step 1 - Install a Virtualisation Platform
docs.text:
Choose a hypervisor that is compatible with your host operating system.

Install it using the instructions provided by the vendor.

Once installed, confirm that you can create a new virtual machine.

Architecture compatibility

Before downloading operating-system images, check that the guest operating system architecture is compatible with your computer and hypervisor.

For example, x64 and ARM systems may require different installation images or virtualisation support.

docs.title: Step 2 - Obtain the Operating System Images
docs.text: You will need installation media for:

docs.title: Windows Server 2022
docs.text:
Download a Windows Server 2022 installation ISO from an official Microsoft source.

This server will later provide:

  • Active Directory Domain Services
  • DNS
  • identity management
  • authentication
  • access control

docs.title: Ubuntu
docs.text:
Download a supported Ubuntu LTS installation image from the official Ubuntu source.

Ubuntu will later act as our integration machine.

We will use it to test:

  • network connectivity
  • DNS
  • LDAP
  • application integration

docs.title: Step 3 - Create the Windows Server VM
docs.text:
Create a new virtual machine and attach the Windows Server ISO.

A reasonable starting configuration is:

Resource Suggested Configuration CPU 2 virtual processors Memory 4-6 GB RAM Disk 40-60 GB Network NAT or shared virtual network

These values are not strict requirements.

You may adjust them depending on the resources available on your host computer.

Do not allocate all of your physical computer's CPU or memory to the VM.

docs.title: Step 4 - Create the Ubuntu VM
docs.text:
Create a second virtual machine and attach the Ubuntu ISO.

A reasonable starting configuration is:

Resource Suggested Configuration CPU 2 virtual processors Memory 4 GB RAM Disk 25-40 GB Network Same virtual network as Windows Server

The important part is the network configuration.

Both virtual machines must eventually be able to communicate with each other.

docs.title: Why Must They Share a Network?
docs.text:
Later, Ubuntu will send requests to Windows Server.

For example:

Ubuntu
   │
   │ LDAP request
   │ TCP 389
   ▼
Windows Server
Active Directory

If the two VMs cannot reach each other over the network, the application integration will fail.

For now, simply ensure that both VMs use the same virtual networking mode.

We will examine IP addresses, subnets, gateways, DNS, and connectivity in the Networking lesson.

docs.title: Step 5 - Install the Operating Systems
docs.text:
Start both virtual machines and install their operating systems from the ISO images.

At this stage, the objective is simply to reach a working operating system on each VM.

The Windows Server configuration will be covered in the next lesson.

docs.title: Step 6 - Check Your Environment
docs.text:
You should now have something similar to:

Host Computer
        │
        └── Virtualisation Platform
                │
                ├── Windows Server 2022
                │
                └── Ubuntu

Confirm that:

  • both virtual machines start successfully
  • Windows Server reaches its login screen
  • Ubuntu reaches its login screen
  • both VMs have a virtual network adapter
  • neither VM consumes all of the host computer's resources

docs.title: Optional - Create a Snapshot
docs.text:
If your hypervisor supports snapshots, this is a useful time to create one.

A snapshot records the current state of a virtual machine.

If something breaks later, you may be able to return to this clean state instead of reinstalling the operating system.

A useful snapshot name might be:

Clean OS Installation

Snapshots are useful for labs, but they should not be treated as a replacement for proper backups in production environments.

docs.title: What You Should Understand
docs.text:
Before moving on, make sure you can explain the following in your own words:

What is the difference between a host and a guest?

The host is the physical computer. The guest is an operating system running inside a virtual machine.

What does a hypervisor do?

It creates and manages virtual machines and allocates resources such as CPU, memory, disks, and networking.

Why are we using two virtual machines?

Because we want to simulate separate systems communicating across a network, rather than installing everything on one computer.

Why must Windows Server and Ubuntu be able to communicate?

Because Ubuntu will later behave like an external system integrating with services hosted by Windows Server.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
Without looking at the diagram, try to explain this architecture:

Host
  ↓
Hypervisor
  ↓
Windows Server + Ubuntu
  ↓
Network communication
  ↓
Software integration

If you can explain why each layer exists, you understand the foundation of the project.

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text:
The virtual infrastructure is ready.

Next, we will configure the Windows Server that will become the hospital Domain Controller.

Continue to Windows Server →

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
In this lesson, you will install and prepare Windows Server 2022 for the hospital identity environment.

Later, this server will become the Domain Controller responsible for services such as:

  • Active Directory Domain Services
  • DNS
  • user authentication
  • identity management
  • group-based access control

At this stage, we are only preparing the operating system.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
You should already have:

  • a virtualisation platform installed
  • a Windows Server virtual machine
  • a Windows Server 2022 installation ISO attached to the VM
  • sufficient CPU, memory, and disk resources allocated

If you have not created the VM yet, complete the Virtualisation Setup lesson first.

docs.title: Step 1 - Start the Windows Server VM
docs.text:
Start the virtual machine containing the Windows Server ISO.

The VM should boot into the Windows Server installation environment.

Select your:

  • language
  • time and currency format
  • keyboard layout

Then continue to the installation screen.

docs.title: Step 2 - Choose the Windows Server Edition
docs.text:
Depending on the installation media, several editions may appear.

For a beginner-friendly environment, choose a version that includes:

Desktop Experience

For example:

Windows Server 2022 Standard Evaluation
(Desktop Experience)

docs.title: Desktop Experience vs Server Core
docs.text:
Desktop Experience provides the familiar Windows graphical interface.

Server Core provides a minimal installation without the traditional desktop interface and is normally administered primarily through command-line tools and remote management.

For this project, Desktop Experience makes it easier to explore tools such as:

  • Server Manager
  • Active Directory Users and Computers
  • DNS Manager
  • Computer Management

docs.title: Step 3 - Choose the Installation Type
docs.text:
When Windows asks which type of installation you want, choose:

Custom: Install Microsoft Server Operating System only

A custom installation is appropriate because we are creating a new server rather than upgrading an existing Windows installation.

docs.title: Step 4 - Select the Virtual Disk
docs.text:
Windows will display the virtual disk created for the VM.

Select the available unallocated disk space and continue.

For this learning environment, a virtual disk of approximately 40-60 GB is normally sufficient.

Windows will automatically create the partitions required for the operating system.

docs.title: Step 5 - Complete the Installation
docs.text:
Windows Server will copy files and install the operating system.

The virtual machine may restart several times.

After installation, you will be asked to configure the built-in:

Administrator

account.

Create a strong password that you can remember for the lab.

Warning

Do not reuse real passwords from personal, university, or workplace accounts.

This project should use credentials created specifically for the simulated environment.

docs.title: Step 6 - Sign In
docs.text:
After installation is complete, sign in using the Administrator account.

You should reach the Windows Server desktop.

Server Manager will normally open automatically.

Server Manager is one of the main administration tools used to configure Windows Server roles and features.

docs.title: Step 7 - Inspect the Server
docs.text:
Before changing anything, inspect the current system.

Open:

Server Manager → Local Server

Look for information such as:

  • computer name
  • Windows edition
  • network adapter
  • IP address
  • time zone
  • Windows Firewall status
  • remote management status

The objective is to understand the server's current state before configuring it.

docs.title: Step 8 - Check the Computer Name
docs.text:
Every computer on a network needs a hostname.

You can check the current hostname from Command Prompt:

hostname

You can also use PowerShell:

$env:COMPUTERNAME

The default hostname generated by Windows may not be very meaningful.

Later, you may rename the server to something easier to recognise, such as:

DC01

This naming convention can help identify the machine as the first Domain Controller in the environment.

docs.title: Step 9 - Inspect the Network Configuration
docs.text:
Open Command Prompt and run:

ipconfig

Look for:

  • IPv4 Address
  • Subnet Mask
  • Default Gateway
  • DNS Servers

Do not worry if the address was automatically assigned.

In the next lesson, we will examine how IP addressing, DNS, DHCP and virtual networking affect communication between the Windows Server and Ubuntu machines.

docs.title: Step 10 - Check Internet Connectivity
docs.text:
If your virtualisation network provides internet access, test connectivity.

For example:

ping 8.8.8.8

You can also test DNS resolution:

nslookup microsoft.com

These tests answer two different questions.

ping 8.8.8.8 helps test basic IP connectivity.

nslookup microsoft.com helps verify that DNS name resolution is working.

docs.title: Optional - Create a Snapshot
docs.text:
Once Windows Server is installed and working, consider creating a virtual machine snapshot.

A useful snapshot name could be:

Windows Server Clean Install

This gives you a recovery point before making major configuration changes.

docs.title: What You Should Understand
docs.text:
Before continuing, make sure you can explain:

Why are we using Windows Server instead of normal Windows?

Windows Server provides enterprise services such as Active Directory Domain Services, DNS, centralized authentication, and server roles.

What is Server Manager?

Server Manager is an administration interface used to configure and monitor Windows Server.

Why do we inspect the network before configuring Active Directory?

Active Directory depends heavily on reliable networking and DNS.

If network configuration is incorrect, authentication and directory services may fail later.

Why are we not configuring Active Directory yet?

We are separating the project into layers.

First we establish the server.

Then we configure networking.

After networking is understood and verified, we add the identity services.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Before moving on, confirm that:

  • Windows Server boots successfully
  • you can sign in as Administrator
  • Server Manager opens
  • the server has a hostname
  • the server has an IP address
  • you can inspect its network configuration
  • the virtual network adapter is working

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
Using only the tools available inside Windows Server, find:

  1. your hostname
  2. your IPv4 address
  3. your default gateway
  4. your DNS server
  5. your Windows Server edition

Try to explain what each value represents rather than simply copying it.

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text:
The Windows Server operating system is ready.

Next, we will configure the network so that Windows Server and the Ubuntu integration machine can reliably communicate.

Continue to Networking →

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
In this lesson, you will configure and test the network that connects the Windows Server and Ubuntu virtual machines.

By the end of the lesson, you should understand:

  • IP addresses
  • subnet masks
  • default gateways
  • DHCP
  • static IP addresses
  • NAT
  • DNS
  • basic connectivity testing

You will also prepare the Windows Server for its future role as a Domain Controller.

docs.title: Why Networking Matters
docs.text:
Our environment contains separate virtual machines:

Host Computer
        │
        └── Virtual Network
                │
                ├── Windows Server
                │
                └── Ubuntu

Later, Ubuntu will need to communicate with services running on Windows Server.

For example:

Ubuntu
   │
   │ LDAP request
   │ TCP 389
   ▼
Windows Server
Active Directory

If the network is configured incorrectly, the application may appear to have an authentication or LDAP problem when the real issue is simply connectivity.

This is why networking should be verified before application integration begins.

docs.title: IP Address
docs.text:
An IP address identifies a device on a network.

For example:

192.168.100.10

Think of it as the network address of a computer.

docs.title: Subnet Mask
docs.text:
The subnet mask helps determine which devices belong to the same local network.

A common subnet mask is:

255.255.255.0

This is also written as:

/24

For example:

192.168.100.10/24
192.168.100.20/24

normally belong to the same local subnet.

docs.title: Default Gateway
docs.text:
The default gateway is the device that allows traffic to leave the local network.

For example:

192.168.100.1

If a machine needs to communicate with a destination outside its local subnet, it normally sends the traffic to its default gateway.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
DNS stands for Domain Name System.

DNS translates names into IP addresses.

For example:

microsoft.com
        ↓
IP address

In an Active Directory environment, DNS becomes even more important because computers use DNS to locate services such as Domain Controllers.

docs.title: DHCP
docs.text:
DHCP stands for Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol.

A DHCP server can automatically provide a computer with:

  • an IP address
  • subnet mask
  • default gateway
  • DNS configuration

This is convenient for normal client devices.

However, servers often use static addresses because other systems need to know where to find them consistently.

docs.title: Static IP Address
docs.text:
A static IP address does not change automatically.

A Domain Controller should normally have a predictable address.

For example:

Windows Server
192.168.100.10

Other machines can then consistently contact that server.

docs.title: NAT
docs.text:
NAT stands for Network Address Translation.

Many virtualisation platforms use NAT to allow virtual machines to access external networks through the host computer.

A simplified view looks like:

Virtual Machine
      │
      ▼
Virtual NAT Network
      │
      ▼
Host Computer
      │
      ▼
Internet

The virtual machine has its own private IP address, while the hypervisor translates traffic when it leaves the virtual network.

docs.title: Step 1 - Check the Virtual Network
docs.text:
Before configuring IP addresses, verify that both virtual machines use the same virtual networking mode.

Depending on your hypervisor, you may see options such as:

  • NAT
  • Shared Network
  • Bridged
  • Host-only

For this project, the important requirement is:

Windows Server and Ubuntu must be able to communicate with each other.

Note

The exact names of networking modes vary between VMware, VirtualBox, Hyper-V and other hypervisors.

Focus on the network architecture rather than a specific product interface.

docs.title: Step 2 - Inspect Windows Server Networking
docs.text:
Open Command Prompt or PowerShell on Windows Server.

Run:

ipconfig

For more detailed information:

ipconfig /all

Look for:

  • IPv4 Address
  • Subnet Mask
  • Default Gateway
  • DNS Servers
  • DHCP Enabled

Example:

IPv4 Address:      192.168.100.20
Subnet Mask:       255.255.255.0
Default Gateway:   192.168.100.1

Your values will probably be different.

Do not copy example IP addresses directly into your environment.

docs.title: Step 3 - Inspect Ubuntu Networking
docs.text:
On Ubuntu, open Terminal.

Run:

ip addr

This displays the network interfaces and their IP addresses.

You can also check the routing table:

ip route

You may see something similar to:

default via 192.168.100.1

This identifies the default gateway.

To inspect DNS configuration on many modern Ubuntu systems, use:

resolvectl status

docs.title: Step 4 - Compare the Two Machines
docs.text:
Record the important information from both machines.

For example:

Setting Windows Server Ubuntu IPv4 192.168.100.10 192.168.100.20 Subnet /24 /24 Gateway 192.168.100.1 192.168.100.1 Network 192.168.100.0 192.168.100.0

If both machines are on the same subnet, they should normally be able to communicate directly.

docs.title: Step 5 - Test the Default Gateway
docs.text:
From Windows Server:

ping <gateway-ip>

For example:

ping 192.168.100.1

From Ubuntu:

ping -c 4 <gateway-ip>

If the gateway responds, the local network path is working.

Note

A failed ping does not always prove that a device is unreachable.

Firewalls can block ICMP traffic while other services continue to work.

Ping is one diagnostic tool, not a complete connectivity test.

docs.title: Step 6 - Test Internet Connectivity
docs.text:
An important troubleshooting technique is to separate IP connectivity from DNS resolution.

First, test an external IP address.

Windows:

ping 8.8.8.8

Ubuntu:

ping -c 4 8.8.8.8

If this works, external IP connectivity exists.

Now test a hostname.

Windows:

nslookup microsoft.com

Ubuntu:

nslookup microsoft.com

If the IP test works but the hostname lookup fails, the problem is likely related to DNS rather than basic network connectivity.

docs.title: Step 7 - Give the Windows Server a Static IP
docs.text:
A Domain Controller should have a stable network address.

Before changing anything, record the settings received through DHCP:

  • current IP address
  • subnet mask
  • default gateway
  • DNS server

Then select an appropriate unused address inside the same subnet.

For example:

IP address:      192.168.100.10
Subnet mask:     255.255.255.0
Default gateway: 192.168.100.1

Warning

These are example addresses only.

Your virtual network may use a completely different range.

Always inspect your existing network before selecting a static IP address.

On Windows Server, open:

Server Manager → Local Server → Ethernet

Then open the network adapter properties.

Select:

Internet Protocol Version 4 (TCP/IPv4)

and configure the chosen static address.

docs.title: Why Does the Server Need a Static Address?
docs.text:
Imagine Ubuntu is configured to contact:

192.168.100.10

If DHCP later changes the Windows Server address to:

192.168.100.35

Ubuntu may continue trying to contact the old address.

The integration would fail.

A static IP gives important infrastructure a predictable location.

docs.title: Step 8 - Verify the Static Configuration
docs.text:
After changing the address, run:

ipconfig /all

Confirm that:

  • the expected IPv4 address appears
  • the subnet mask is correct
  • the gateway is correct

Then test the gateway again:

ping <gateway-ip>

And test external connectivity:

ping 8.8.8.8

docs.title: Step 9 - Understand DNS in Active Directory
docs.text:
DNS is particularly important in this project.

Normal internet DNS may resolve names such as:

microsoft.com
ubuntu.com
github.com

Active Directory DNS will later also resolve internal names such as:

hospital.local
dc01.hospital.local

After the server becomes a Domain Controller with DNS installed, domain members should use the Active Directory DNS server so they can locate domain services.

A simplified architecture will eventually look like:

Ubuntu / Client
      │
      │ DNS query
      ▼
Windows Server
Active Directory DNS
      │
      ▼
Domain services

We will configure this further during the Active Directory stage.

docs.title: Step 10 - Test Communication Between the VMs
docs.text:
Now test communication between Windows Server and Ubuntu.

First find Ubuntu's address:

ip addr

From Windows Server:

ping <ubuntu-ip>

Then find the Windows Server address:

ipconfig

From Ubuntu:

ping -c 4 <windows-server-ip>

If both machines can reach each other, the basic network path is ready.

docs.title: A Better Troubleshooting Method
docs.text:
When something does not work, avoid testing everything at once.

Work through the network layer by layer.

docs.title: 1. Does the machine have an IP address?
docs.text:
Windows:

ipconfig

Ubuntu:

ip addr

docs.title: 2. Can it reach its gateway?
docs.text:
Machine
   ↓
Gateway

docs.title: 3. Can it reach another IP address?
docs.text:
Windows Server
      ↓
Ubuntu

docs.title: 4. Can it reach the internet by IP?
docs.text: ping 8.8.8.8

docs.title: 5. Can DNS resolve names?
docs.text: nslookup microsoft.com

docs.title: 6. Can the application port be reached?
docs.text:
Later, we may test specific services such as:

LDAP  → TCP 389
LDAPS → TCP 636
SMB   → TCP 445

This layered approach helps identify where the failure occurs.

docs.title: Common Problems
docs.text: Symptom Possible Cause No IP address Network adapter or DHCP problem Cannot reach gateway Virtual network or IP configuration problem Can reach IP but not hostname DNS problem Windows and Ubuntu cannot communicate Different networks, firewall, or addressing issue Server address changes DHCP still being used Internet works but domain services fail Internal DNS configuration may be incorrect Ping fails but application works ICMP may be blocked by a firewall

docs.title: DHCP vs Static IP
docs.text: A useful way to remember the difference:

docs.title: DHCP
docs.text:
Device starts
     ↓
Requests configuration
     ↓
DHCP provides IP settings

Good for:

  • laptops
  • desktops
  • temporary clients
  • general user devices

docs.title: Static IP
docs.text:
Administrator chooses address
          ↓
Address remains predictable

Commonly used for infrastructure such as:

  • servers
  • Domain Controllers
  • DNS servers
  • network appliances

docs.title: What You Should Understand
docs.text:
Before continuing, make sure you can explain:

What does an IP address do?

It identifies a network interface so other systems know where to send traffic.

What does the subnet mask do?

It helps determine which portion of an IP address identifies the network and which portion identifies the host.

What is the default gateway?

It provides a route toward destinations outside the local subnet.

What does DHCP do?

It automatically provides network configuration to clients.

Why do we give the Domain Controller a static IP?

Because other systems need a predictable address for services such as DNS and authentication.

What does DNS do?

It resolves names into IP addresses and, in Active Directory, helps systems locate domain services.

What does NAT do?

It translates network traffic between address spaces, allowing virtual machines on private networks to communicate with external networks through the host or hypervisor.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
Before moving on, confirm that:

  • Windows Server has an IP address
  • Ubuntu has an IP address
  • both machines are on compatible virtual networks
  • you know the subnet mask
  • you know the default gateway
  • Windows Server has a stable IP address
  • the machines can test local connectivity
  • DNS resolution can be tested
  • you understand the difference between DHCP and static addressing

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
Without looking back at the definitions, explain what happens when Ubuntu tries to communicate with the Windows Server.

Use these terms:

  • IP address
  • subnet
  • network adapter
  • DNS
  • gateway

Then answer this troubleshooting scenario:

ping 8.8.8.8
SUCCESS

nslookup microsoft.com
FAIL

Which network service would you investigate first?

Answer: DNS.

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text:
The network foundation is ready.

Next, we will turn Windows Server into the identity system for the simulated hospital by installing and configuring Active Directory Domain Services.

Continue to Active Directory →
